message.content:
Design a 50-question training curriculum for the Boldteq HR Department (6 agents: Cadence, Roster, Witness, Forge, Tutor, Mira) so they coordinate flawlessly at 54-agent scale, like a Fortune-500 People Ops team.

Goal: Each question I ask Yash must produce a binding decision he can ratify, then Mira/Tutor codify into the agent prompts. Output is a curriculum that closes real coordination gaps, not theoretical ones.

USE THESE EXACT GAPS (already mapped from exploration):

GAP 1 — HR Cross-Agent Conflict Resolution:
- Witness flags PIP, Cadence disagrees → no tie-breaker
- Tutor patch fires while Witness is mid-flagging same agent → no interlock
- Roster vetoes dispatch but task is critical → no escalation SLA
- Forge auto-deploys, Cadence finds duplicate mandate post-hoc → no pre-check

GAP 2 — Stale Data / Latency:
- Cadence reviews weekly Mondays only; agent could fail Wed-Fri and not be flagged for 6 days
- Composite score uses last 20 runs — no freshness guard
- Probation 10-run window; Witness watches but no parallelization protocol for 5 simultaneous probation agents

GAP 3 — Wrongful Action Guards:
- No appeal process for Witness antipattern false positives
- No data-freshness check before Cadence opens 14-day PIP
- No duplicate-mandate detection before Forge hires
- No rollback authority if Tutor patch worsens performance

GAP 4 — Real-time vs Polling:
- Schema mentions Supabase Realtime but no channels defined
- Tutor measures impact 48h post-patch — what if 2 patches land on same agent in 6h?
- No interrupt mechanism for in-flight agent if critical patch must apply now

GAP 5 — Memory Decay + Knowledge Hygiene:
- Patterns >90 days unused — no auto-archive trigger
- Mira pattern conflicts kept "with context" — no resolution SLA
- Duplicate signal detection (Witness + Mira flag same lesson) not enforced

GAP 6 — Scale & Load:
- 54 agents weekly review — peer-avg cache strategy missing
- Forge cohort hire 5 agents/week — onboarding parallelization not documented
- No SLO/SLA for any HR loop (latency to flag, time-to-PIP, time-to-promote)

GAP 7 — Authority & RACI:
- HR agents are PARALLEL watchers, not pipelined → no clear arbitration
- "Earlier in pipeline wins" rule does NOT apply to HR
- Yash escalation criteria undefined (when does HR auto-decide vs ping Yash?)

GAP 8 — Production Quality:
- Witness false-positive: no human review gate before incident escalation to Verdict
- Composite score edge cases (<5 runs, status mid-change, probation level 1) undocumented
- Cost overrun handling mid-task — Tutor reaction timing unclear

DELIVERABLE:
Draft 50 multiple-choice questions organized into 10 themes (5 questions each):
1. Conflict Arbitration (HR cross-agent disagreement)
2. Decision Authority & RACI (who decides what, when does Yash get pinged)
3. Data Freshness & Latency SLAs (max age for PIP/promote/hire decisions)
4. Wrongful Action Guards (PIP/hire/patch reversibility, appeals)
5. Real-Time vs Batch (Supabase Realtime channels, interrupt mechanisms)
6. Probation & Onboarding at Scale (5/week parallelization)
7. Training Patch Attribution & Rollback (cross-patch impact)
8. Memory Hygiene & Decay (archive triggers, conflict resolution SLA)
9. Cost & Wall-Clock Safety (per-agent budgets, breaker thresholds)
10. Org Health Metrics (north-star for HR dept itself, weekly health report)

For EACH of the 50 questions, provide:
- Question text (clear, single decision)
- 3-4 options labeled A/B/C/D
- **Recommended answer** with 1-2 sentence rationale grounded in production People-Ops practice (Fortune-500 patterns: SLAs, peer-review tribunals, blameless post-mortems, 360 reviews, comp committees, calibration sessions, etc.)

Do NOT write production code or settings files. This is a planning artifact only.

Output format: Markdown table or numbered list. Compact but complete — Yash will read all 50 questions in one sitting and pick.

Write your output as a plan file to /Users/yashbaldha/.claude/plans/so-for-hr-department-clever-bumblebee.md (the user is in plan mode and this is the only file I can write to). Use this structure:

# HR Department Training Curriculum — 50 Decisions

## Context
[Why this matters — 3 sentences max]

## How To Use
[Yash answers each Q with letter + optional override; Mira codifies into agent prompts; Tutor ships patches; Cadence ratifies via weekly review]

## Theme 1: Conflict Arbitration (Q1-5)
### Q1: [question]
- A) ...
- B) ...
- C) ...
- D) ...
**Recommended: B** — [rationale]

[...continue for all 50]

## Verification
[How we test: dry-run weekly cycle with 54-agent fixture, replay 30d historical incidents, measure decision latency + false-positive rate]

## Critical Files To Update Post-Decision
[List the 6 agent .md files + agent-ops-schema.md + new HR runbook to create]

Keep questions sharp, options mutually exclusive, recommendations grounded in real People-Ops practice. Total file should be ~1500-2000 lines.

# HR Department Training Curriculum — 50 Decisions

## Context
The Boldteq HR Department (Cadence, Roster, Witness, Forge, Tutor, Mira) operates as parallel watchers over a 54-agent workforce, but the current prompts at `/Users/yashbaldha/.claude/agents/{cadence,roster,witness,forge,tutor,mira}.md` were written for ~12 agents and lack arbitration, freshness SLAs, and rollback authority. At 54-agent scale, ambiguity becomes outage: PIPs fire on stale data, patches collide mid-flight, Forge ships duplicates, and Yash gets paged for noise instead of decisions. This curriculum closes 8 mapped coordination gaps with 50 binding decisions modeled on Fortune-500 People Ops practice (calibration sessions, comp committees, blameless post-mortems, RACI matrices, peer-review tribunals).

## How To Use
1. Yash reads all 50 questions in one sitting and answers each with a letter (A/B/C/D), optionally with a free-text override.
2. Mira codifies each ratified answer into the relevant agent prompt section (anchors listed per question).
3. Tutor ships the prompt patches in a single coordinated PR (one commit per agent, training_signal P1, 48h impact window).
4. Cadence ratifies the patch lot at the next Monday 09:00 UTC review and logs the decision-set in `agent_reviews`.
5. Roster regenerates the registry skill index so any new RACI/SLA shows up in `experience.profiles[*].hr_protocol`.
6. The 50 answers become the **HR Constitution v1** — version-pinned, immutable except by re-vote.

---

## Theme 1: Conflict Arbitration (Q1–5)

### Q1: Witness flags an agent for PIP based on antipattern frequency. Cadence's weekly review concludes the same agent's composite score is trending up and recommends "monitor only." Who wins?
- A) Witness wins — accountability layer always overrides director recommendation; PIP fires immediately.
- B) Cadence wins — director has final say on lifecycle state; Witness re-evaluates next sweep.
- C) Tie-breaker tribunal — both signals queue to a 48h `hr_arbitration` table; Yash decides if no consensus emerges via shared `composite_score + antipattern_density` rubric.
- D) Auto-escalate to Yash on any Witness/Cadence delta — no autonomous arbitration.

**Recommended: C** — Fortune-500 calibration sessions resolve manager-vs-data conflicts via a structured 48h cool-down with a shared rubric, not unilateral override. C preserves both signals, prevents thrash, and only escalates true deadlocks to the executive. A causes false-positive PIPs; B masks real performance decay; D paralyzes the loop at scale.

### Q2: Tutor begins applying a P1 training patch to agent X at 14:02. Witness is mid-classification of agent X's 14:00 run and is about to flag an antipattern at 14:04. What's the interlock?
- A) First-writer-wins — whichever agent's transaction commits first; the other aborts and retries.
- B) Tutor holds a `training_lock` on the target agent; Witness queues its flag, applies it post-patch with a 24h re-evaluation window.
- C) Witness holds priority — Tutor must wait for "no flags pending" green light before any patch.
- D) Both proceed independently; reconciliation happens at next Cadence weekly review.

**Recommended: B** — Production People-Ops never lets training and discipline land on the same employee in the same hour without a 24h observation window — patches change behavior, so pre-patch antipattern signals must be re-validated post-patch. B implements a real lock with explicit re-evaluation, mirroring HRIS change-freeze patterns.

### Q3: Roster vetoes a dispatch ("agent Y lacks skill Z"), but Yash flagged the task as P0/critical with a 1h deadline. Escalation path?
- A) Veto stands — Roster is source of truth; task fails the SLA, Cadence reviews next week.
- B) Veto is downgraded to a warning — task proceeds, Witness watches the run with hair-trigger antipattern detection, Forge auto-drafts a remediation training_signal regardless of outcome.
- C) Yash gets paged immediately with a 5-min decision window: override or accept fail.
- D) Cadence performs an emergency reassignment to nearest-skill peer; Roster veto logged but bypassed.

**Recommended: B** — Fortune-500 P0 incident protocols prefer "proceed with monitoring" over hard-fail when an SLA breach is the alternative. B preserves the signal (Roster's veto is logged and triggers Forge), limits the blast radius (Witness watches), and avoids waking Yash for every P0. C is right only if cost of failure > $X — define that threshold in Q21.

### Q4: Forge auto-deploys a new agent at 02:00 UTC. Cadence's Monday review at 09:00 UTC discovers the new agent duplicates 80% of an existing agent's mandate. What's the protocol?
- A) Forge has commit-and-review authority — duplicate is retired by Cadence, Forge gets a training_signal but no rollback.
- B) Pre-deploy diff gate — Forge must run a 4-axis similarity check (skills, tools, model, mandate) against `registry.json` and request Cadence sign-off if ≥60% overlap with any active agent.
- C) Auto-merge — duplicate is consolidated into existing agent via prompt union; Forge's draft becomes a patch instead of a hire.
- D) Yash approves all hires — remove Forge's auto-deploy authority entirely.

**Recommended: B** — Comp committees never approve a new req without a "is this a duplicate role" sign-off; same logic applies to agent hires. B keeps Forge's autonomy for genuinely-new capabilities while installing the cheapest possible duplicate-detection check. D destroys the whole point of Forge; A is reactive and wastes a probation slot.

### Q5: Mira detects a pattern conflict (one "good" pattern contradicts another "good" pattern) for the 3rd time in 30 days. Resolution?
- A) Last-write-wins — newer pattern marked canonical, older deprecated.
- B) Mira opens a `pattern_conflict` ticket with 7-day Yash-decision SLA; both patterns marked `contested` until resolved; agents prefer the higher-confidence one in the meantime.
- C) Both patterns kept "with context tags" indefinitely; agents use whichever matches their context.
- D) Cadence breaks the tie at weekly review using outcome data from agents that used each pattern.

**Recommended: B** — Engineering style guides at scale (Google, Stripe) use a "contested → SLA → ratify" flow precisely because keeping two contradicting rules live causes silent drift. B forces resolution within a week with an explicit fallback rule (higher-confidence wins in interim) instead of letting C's accumulated ambiguity rot the brain.

---

## Theme 2: Decision Authority & RACI (Q6–10)

### Q6: When does HR decide autonomously vs. ping Yash? Define the universal rule.
- A) HR auto-decides everything; Yash is informed via a daily digest only.
- B) Yash approves every PIP, every hire, every patch — full manual oversight.
- C) **Cost/risk-tiered RACI**: HR auto-decides if (cost-impact < $50/wk) AND (reversible in <24h) AND (no Yash-tagged "ratification-required" agent). Otherwise queues to Yash with a 24h decision SLA.
- D) HR auto-decides for Probation-level agents only; Active agents always need Yash.

**Recommended: C** — Standard People-Ops delegation matrix: managers act within budget + reversibility envelope; exec ratifies only above the threshold. C scales to 54 agents (B does not) and avoids hidden runaway costs (A lets that happen). The $50/wk + 24h-reversible bar matches typical Director-level discretion.

### Q7: Who owns the final call on **promote-to-Active**?
- A) Witness — they have the run-level data.
- B) Cadence — director role per current spec.
- C) Cadence proposes, Yash ratifies (single-click approve), Roster commits to registry; Witness has veto if antipattern_density >5% in last 30 runs.
- D) Cohort calibration — promote in batches at end-of-month review with all 6 HR agents voting.

- D) Last 7 days only.

**Recommended: C** — Performance Improvement Plans built on stale data are legally and ethically indefensible in human HR; same logic for agents. ### Q12: Witness daily sweep currently runs 03:00 UTC. What's the new cadence?
- A) Keep daily 03:00 UTC.
- B) **Twice-daily (03:00 + 15:00 UTC)** plus event-triggered re-sweep on any agent with >5 runs in past 60 min.
- C) Real-time only — no batch sweep, every run classified as it lands via Supabase Realtime trigger.
- D) Hourly batch sweep.

**Recommended: B** — Mature ops teams blend batch (cheap, predictable) with event-triggered real-time (catches bursts) — pure batch has 24h blind spot, pure real-time is expensive on Haiku tier. B closes Gap 2's Wed-Fri window while keeping Witness's CHEAP model assignment cost-effective.

- D) Use last 50 runs regardless of date.

**Recommended: C** — Promotion decisions need both recency (3-day) and stability (low variance) — promoting a high-scoring but volatile agent is the classic "regression to the mean" trap. C combines a freshness floor with a volatility check, mirroring how comp committees weight both performance and consistency.

### Q14: Roster nightly recompute (02:00 UTC) — is that fresh enough for dispatch decisions?
- A) Yes, 24h-old experience profiles are fine for dispatch.
- B) **No — add a 5-min cache invalidation on `agent_runs` insert; dispatch must read profile generated within last 6h, else trigger sync recompute.**
- C) Recompute every hour.
- D) Real-time recompute on every run completion.

**Recommended: B** — Cache invalidation is the cheapest fix for staleness — full hourly recompute is wasteful, real-time is overkill. B uses an event-driven invalidation pattern (mature in HRIS systems) to guarantee dispatches never use stale skill profiles, with a 6h ceiling for safety.

### Q15: Define HR loop SLAs (the 4 numbers that define "healthy").

- D) Yash defines SLAs per-agent ad hoc.

**Recommended: C** — SRE-style SLOs with error budgets are the only way HR can know if it's actually healthy. C names the four loops, sets p95 targets (matches industry SLO practice), and bakes in quarterly review — error budgets force rebalancing instead of perpetual heroics.

- C) Yash approves every patch.

**Recommended: B** — Production deploy gates use pre-flight simulation + post-deploy guardrails. - D) No mid-task breaker; reconcile at end-of-task only.

**Recommended: C** — Tiered circuit breakers (warn → graceful → hard) are the only safe pattern for cost-sensitive systems; binary kill-switches lose work. - D) Always allow; ignore attribution.

- C) Always hard kill in-flight runs for P0 patches.
- D) P0 patches are forbidden mid-flight; all patches are post-task.

**Recommended: B** — Hybrid batch+event is the modern HR data-pipeline pattern: decisions that benefit from batched context (Cadence, Mira) stay batch; decisions that need fast reaction (Witness, Tutor, Forge) go event-driven. B aligns the architecture with the actual decision latency requirement of each agent.

**Recommended: B** — Standard pattern for any event-driven system: realtime is the optimization, polling is the truth. B guarantees correctness via fallback (no lost events), tracks SLO (99.5% matches typical Supabase Realtime), and only escalates if uptime trend breaks the budget — not on every blip.

## Theme 6: Probation & Onboarding at Scale (Q26–30)

- C) Hire only 1 agent per week.
- D) Cadence handles probation tracking instead of Witness when cohort >2.

**Recommended: B** — The People-Ops pattern for cohort onboarding (e.g., new-grad classes at FAANG) is parallel individual tracking + cohort-level pattern detection. B preserves individual scoring while catching cohort-class issues (e.g., "all 5 hires miss the same antipattern" = template defect, not 5 separate patches).

### Q27: Probation graduation criteria — when does a probationary agent become Active?
- A) After 10 runs, regardless of score.
- B) After 10 runs with composite score ≥ peer-average.

- D) After 30 days regardless of run count.

**Recommended: C** — Real onboarding completion criteria are multi-axis: meets bar, no recent failures, recent stability, manager sign-off. C is rigorous without being arbitrary, and the "+5 runs OR retire" path mirrors real probation extension policy.

### Q28: Probation level 1 (a fresh hire's very first run) — how does composite score get computed when there's only 1 data point?
- A) Use the score of the single run as composite.
- B) **Composite undefined until ≥5 runs; agent shown as `score_pending` in dashboards. For the first 5 runs, Witness compares to template-cohort baseline (other agents from same Forge template) instead of peer-average. After 5 runs, switch to standard composite.**
- C) Use a "default new-hire" score of 0.7.
- D) Don't accept dispatches until 5 runs of synthetic test data.

**Recommended: B** — Statistical honesty: small samples don't have means. B uses a cohort baseline (what similar agents scored at run-1..5) instead of pretending a single point is signal — this is the standard method in performance analytics for new hires (compare to similar tenure cohort, not all-employee average).

### Q29: 5 simultaneous probation agents fail to graduate in same week. Triage?
- A) Retire all 5.

Decision tree drives action: template fix → patch + new cohort, routing fix → Roster patch + retain agents on extended probation, criteria fix → recalibrate baseline.**
- C) Extend all by 5 runs; no investigation.
- D) Yash decides each individually.

**Recommended: B** — When >50% of a cohort fails, the system is broken, not the individuals. B applies the blameless post-mortem pattern (Etsy/Google SRE) to HR — investigates 4 possible root causes before disciplining anyone. This is the pattern that prevents firing-spirals from masking systemic defects.

### Q30: Onboarding documentation per new hire — what gets generated and where?

- B) **Forge generates a 4-artifact onboarding package: (i) agent .md prompt, (ii) `agents/onboarding/{name}-charter.md` (mandate, success criteria, peer-avg targets), (iii) `agents/onboarding/{name}-runbook.md` (escalation paths, owned channels), (iv) entry in `registry.json` with probation flag. Mira links the package to relevant good-patterns.**
- C) Just .md plus registry entry.
- D) Generated post-graduation only.

**Recommended: B** — Real onboarding has more than a job description: charter, runbook, manager-handbook entry, peer-network introduction. B mirrors the structure (4 artifacts, all generated at hire-time) so probationary agents know exactly what success looks like — which makes Q27's evaluation criteria actually fair.

## Theme 7: Training Patch Attribution & Rollback (Q31–35)

### Q31: A patch lands on agent A. 3 days later, agent B (which shares 80% of agent A's prompt template) starts regressing. Cross-attribution?
- A) Coincidence — no auto-link; investigate if pattern continues.
- B) **Tutor maintains a `prompt_lineage` graph; any patch on one agent triggers a 7-day "lineage watch" on all template-siblings (similarity ≥0.7); regression in any sibling auto-links to the original patch and triggers re-evaluation.**
- C) Roll back any patch that has any sibling regression in 7 days.
- D) Don't share templates — fork each agent.

**Recommended: B** — Software supply chain attribution: if you patch a shared library, you watch all consumers. B applies the same logic to prompt templates — sibling watch is cheap (just a join), surfaces hidden coupling, but doesn't auto-rollback (which D-style overreaction would do). This addresses the prompt-template coupling that emerges at 54-agent scale.

### Q32: Patch rollback — does it restore the literal old prompt, or re-derive from current best patterns?
- A) Literal restore from `agent-versions/`.
- B) **Literal restore from `agent-versions/{agent}/{timestamp}.md` AND a new `rollback_signal` is filed for Mira: "patterns that contributed to bad patch should be re-evaluated." Original patch author notified. If same pattern triggers a 2nd rollback in 30d, pattern marked `contested` per Q5.**
- C) Re-derive from current best patterns.
- D) Yash hand-edits.

**Recommended: B** — Rollbacks should be deterministic (literal restore = no surprise) AND a learning event (rollback signal = pattern reconsideration). B combines both, plus the 2x-in-30d tripwire that catches bad patterns before they hurt a 3rd agent.

### Q33: Patch authorship — when Tutor ships 10 patches in a single weekly cycle, how is each one attributed for rollback purposes?
- A) All patches attributed to "Tutor" generically.
- B) **Each patch has: (i) `signal_id` from training_signals table, (ii) `pattern_ids[]` (the brain patterns that contributed), (iii) `prompt_diff` SHA, (iv) `predicted_delta` from Q19's pre-flight, (v) `actual_delta` post-48h. Rollback = revert by `signal_id`.**
- C) Attribute by date only.
- D) Attribute by author Yash for any patches Yash approved.

**Recommended: B** — Full provenance is the only way to learn from rollbacks. B's 5-field attribution lets you answer "was the prediction wrong, was the pattern wrong, or was the diff wrong?" — 3 different fixes. This is standard MLOps experiment tracking applied to prompt patches.

### Q34: Patch chains — patch X → no immediate regression → patch Y on same agent → regression at 24h. Which is at fault?
- A) Patch Y (most recent).
- B) Patch X (only because the 48h window for X hadn't closed).
- C) **Both are tagged `attribution_chain`; auto-revert Y first, observe 24h; if regression persists, also revert X. Both authors get a `chain_attribution_review` task; Mira analyzes which pattern combination caused the issue.**
- D) Roll back to pre-X state immediately.

**Recommended: C** — Bisection-style attribution: peel back the most recent change first, then the older if regression persists. C avoids D's overreaction (potentially undoing 2 good patches) while still resolving in 48h. The `chain_attribution_review` is the learning loop.

### Q35: Patch coverage — what percent of the agent fleet should have a patch in any given month?
- A) 100% — patch every agent monthly.
- B) **Target: 30–50% of fleet receives ≥1 patch per month, prioritized by signal strength (training_signals P0/P1 first); zero-patch agents reviewed quarterly to confirm "stable, not stagnant"; >70% patch rate in a month triggers Cadence "training fatigue" review (too many patches = noise).**
- C) Patch only when explicit signal — no target rate.
- D) Patch every agent every week.

**Recommended: B** — Healthy improvement cadence: enough patches to drive learning (30–50%), not so many that agents are unstable (>70% = fatigue). B mirrors the Spotify "small constant change" model + a stagnation check (zero-patch isn't always good, sometimes it means "we stopped looking"). D causes Q22-style attribution chaos.

Breaches logged to `wall_clock_breaches`; >3 breaches per agent in 7d = Tutor `latency_signal` (could be model-tier mismatch — agent assigned DEEP but doing CHEAP work, or vice versa). Hard timeout = 3× SLO with state save.**
- C) Same SLO for all agents.
- D) Per-task SLO defined at dispatch.

**Recommended: B** — Per-tier SLOs reflect the actual variance — DEEP agents legitimately take longer. B's 3-breach trigger is the canonical "could be a tier mismatch" signal (right-sizing is a major cost lever in any model-routed system). Hard timeout at 3× SLO with state save preserves work.

### Q45: Cost-of-HR — what should the 6 HR agents cost relative to the 48 worker agents?
- A) No constraint.
- B) **HR overhead target: 5–10% of total fleet cost. >15% triggers efficiency review (HR is too expensive for the org it runs); <3% triggers under-investment review (HR may be skipping important checks). Weekly Cadence health report includes the ratio.**
- C) Hard cap 5%.
- D) HR is uncapped — quality first.

**Recommended: B** — Real HR-as-fraction-of-payroll benchmarks run 5–15% in Fortune 500 (varies by industry); B uses 5–10% as a healthy band with both over- and under-investment triggers. The under-investment check is critical — too-cheap HR usually means missed signals, which is a worse failure than overspending.

## Theme 10: Org Health Metrics (Q46–50)

### Q46: HR Department north-star metric — the single number Yash checks first.
- A) Average composite score across all agents.
- B) **`hr_decision_quality_score` = composite of (i) % autonomous decisions not overturned by Yash in 30d, (ii) p95 SLA attainment per Q15, (iii) false-positive rate on PIPs, (iv) rollback rate per Q35. Single 0–1 number, updated weekly. Target ≥0.85.**
- C) Number of PIPs / promotions / hires per week.
- D) Yash satisfaction survey.

**Recommended: B** — A north-star should measure the *quality* of HR's work, not its volume. B blends 4 dimensions (autonomy, SLA, accuracy, restraint) into one number — like a Fortune-500 People Ops scorecard. Target 0.85 sets a high bar; falling below triggers a Cadence review of which dimension dropped.

### Q47: Weekly HR health report — what's in it and who writes it?
- A) Cadence writes a freeform summary.
- B) **Cadence assembles a 6-section template every Monday 10:00 UTC: (1) North-star score (Q46) + delta, (2) Decisions made (PIPs/promotions/hires/rollbacks counts), (3) SLA attainment per Q15, (4) Top 3 escalations to Yash, (5) Cost-of-HR % (Q45), (6) Open arbitrations + their age. Posted to Yash queue; archived to `org/hr-weekly/{date}.md`.**
- C) Auto-generated dashboard, no narrative.
- D) Quarterly only.

**Recommended: B** — Structured weekly health reports (vs. freeform) are the canonical exec-update pattern — Yash gets the same 6 sections every week and can spot trends instantly. B mirrors a typical CHRO weekly to CEO, with archival for historical comparison.

### Q48: HR-of-HR — who reviews the HR agents themselves?
- A) Yash, manually.
- B) **HR agents are evaluated by the same composite-score machinery they apply to others, with one twist: a quarterly cross-evaluation where each HR agent rates the other 5 on RACI fulfillment (anonymous structured rubric, 1–5 scale per dimension). Cadence aggregates; Yash ratifies any "needs improvement" rating. Cadence's own evaluation done by Yash directly.**
- C) HR agents not evaluated.
- D) External audit yearly.

**Recommended: B** — 360-degree review for HR mirrors how Fortune-500 evaluates People Ops itself: data-driven baseline + peer review + exec sign-off. B closes the "who watches the watchers" gap with a structured (not freeform) peer-review tribunal. Cadence-by-Yash is the natural exception (manager-by-skip-level is standard).

### Q49: Quarterly calibration session — does HR run one?
- A) No.
- B) **Yes — quarterly calibration: all 54 agents reviewed in batches of ~15, all 6 HR agents present, Yash chairs. Goals: (i) re-baseline peer-average targets, (ii) re-rank tier assignments (CHEAP/FAST/DEEP), (iii) decide on stale/dormant agents (retire vs. revive), (iv) update HR Constitution if any of the 50 decisions need re-vote. Output: `org/calibration-{YYYY-Qn}.md`.**
- C) Annual calibration only.
- D) Continuous, no formal session.

**Recommended: B** — Quarterly calibration is the Fortune-500 standard for keeping evaluation criteria honest at scale (the alternative is grade inflation/deflation drift). B's 4 goals are exactly the artifacts that decay over a quarter and need batched re-baselining; this is also the natural cadence to revisit the 50-question Constitution (Q1–Q50) so it doesn't become stale.

### Q50: HR Constitution — what's the meta-protocol for changing the answers to Q1–Q49?
- A) Yash can change any answer any time.
- B) **HR Constitution v1 = the ratified A/B/C/D set from these 50 questions. Amendments require: (i) Mira drafts proposed change with rationale (data-backed), (ii) all 6 HR agents review and rate, (iii) Yash ratifies, (iv) version bumped (v1 → v2), (v) Cadence broadcasts to all 54 agents at next weekly review. Emergency amendments (Yash unilateral) allowed but auto-reviewed at next quarterly calibration. Annual mandatory full re-vote.**
- C) Re-vote every 6 months wholesale.
- D) Constitution is immutable.

**Recommended: B** — A constitution needs both stability (B's amendment process) and flexibility (B's emergency clause + annual re-vote). This is the U.S. corporate-bylaws pattern: hard to change casually, but never frozen. The version bump + broadcast ensures every agent knows which Constitution version is in effect.
